title: Natural Wonders of India: Canyons, Craters, Root Bridges and More
seoTitle: Natural Wonders of India: Canyons, Craters and More | Kudozz Club
metaDescription: India's natural wonders: Gandikota gorge, Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat, Lonar crater, Meghalaya's living root bridges, the Rann of Kutch, Loktak's phumdis and more.
description: A guide to the natural wonders of India: the Gandikota gorge on the Penna, the Marble Rocks and Dhuandhar Falls at Bhedaghat, the Lonar crater lake, Meghalaya's living root bridges and Laitlum canyons, the white salt desert of the Rann of Kutch, Loktak Lake's floating islands, the basalt columns of St Mary's Islands, Baratang's mud volcanoes, and the caves of Borra and Belum, with how and when to visit.
dek: India's most remarkable natural sites include a meteorite crater, marble gorges, floating islands and bridges grown from living roots. Here is where to see them.

hero.alt: The Penna river gorge at Gandikota at sunset, Andhra Pradesh

intro: Some of India's most memorable places are the work of rivers, volcanoes, meteorites and, in Meghalaya, generations of patient villagers. They range from deep river gorges and a crater lake to a salt desert that turns white each winter.
This guide focuses on geological and living wonders you can visit. For waterfalls, lakes and caves in depth, see our dedicated guides.
quickAnswer: India's natural wonders include the Gandikota gorge on the Penna river in Andhra Pradesh, the Marble Rocks gorge at Bhedaghat in Madhya Pradesh, Lonar crater lake in Maharashtra, Meghalaya's living root bridges, the white Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, Loktak Lake's floating phumdis in Manipur, the basalt columns of St Mary's Islands in Karnataka, and the Borra and Belum caves in Andhra Pradesh. Most are best visited from October to March.
takeaways: Lonar is a crater lake formed by a meteorite impact, and a Ramsar wetland.
Meghalaya's living root bridges are on UNESCO's Tentative List.
The Rann of Kutch's white salt flats are best from about November to February.
Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat is best seen by boat, which runs outside the monsoon.
St Mary's Islands off Udupi have striking hexagonal basalt columns.

items.name: Gandikota
body: The Penna river has cut a deep gorge through red sandstone beside an old fort, often called the Grand Canyon of India.

image.alt: The Gandikota gorge on the Penna river
image.caption: Gandikota

items.name: Marble Rocks, Bhedaghat
body: Boat rides between marble cliffs on the Narmada, and the Dhuandhar Falls nearby.

image.alt: The marble cliffs of Bhedaghat on the Narmada
image.caption: Marble Rocks, Bhedaghat

items.name: Laitlum
body: Canyons dropping away from the plateau edge near Shillong.

items.name: Living root bridges
body: Khasi and Jaintia communities train the roots of rubber fig trees across streams; the double-decker bridge at Nongriat is the best known.

items.name: Loktak Lake
body: A large freshwater lake in Manipur dotted with floating phumdis, including the Keibul Lamjao National Park.

items.name: Dawki's Umngot river
body: So clear in winter that boats seem to float above the riverbed.

items.name: Rann of Kutch
body: The white salt desert near the Pakistan border, at its best in winter and under a full moon.

items.name: Lonar
body: A crater lake formed by a meteorite impact, in Buldhana district, with old temples on its slopes.

items.name: St Mary's Islands and Baratang
body: Hexagonal basalt columns off Malpe near Udupi; mud volcanoes and limestone caves in the Andamans.

items.name: Borra and Belum
body: Limestone caves with stalactites in the Araku hills and near Kurnool.

sections.heading: Visiting responsibly
paras: Many of these places are fragile. Do not climb on root bridges beyond what locals allow, stay on marked paths at Lonar and Gandikota, never break off cave formations, and carry all waste out. Some sites are community-managed and charge small fees that support maintenance.

sections.heading: How these wonders formed
paras: Most of these sites record long geological histories. Gandikota and Bhedaghat are river gorges, cut over a very long time by the Penna and the Narmada through sandstone and marble. Lonar formed when a meteorite struck the Deccan basalt. St Mary's Islands' columns formed as lava cooled and cracked. The Rann of Kutch is a seasonal salt marsh, flooded in the monsoon and dried into white crust in winter. The root bridges, by contrast, are human work, grown over decades from living trees.

sections.heading: Seeing several on one trip
list: Bhedaghat with Pachmarhi or Kanha in Madhya Pradesh.
Gandikota with Belum Caves in Andhra Pradesh.
Laitlum, the root bridges and Dawki in a Meghalaya loop.
The white Rann with Dholavira and the Kutch craft villages.

safety: Stay on marked trails and viewpoints, and heed local closures after heavy rain; many accidents at waterfalls and cliffs happen off the path.
Entry rules, timings, permits and seasonal closures change; check the forest department or official site before you go.
Boat rides stop in rough weather and during the monsoon at several sites.

faqs.q: What are the natural wonders of India?
faqs.a: Gandikota, Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat, Lonar crater, the living root bridges, the Rann of Kutch, Loktak Lake and St Mary's Islands are among them.

faqs.q: Which is called the Grand Canyon of India?

faqs.a: By a meteorite impact, which created a crater that now holds a saline lake.

faqs.q: Are the living root bridges a UNESCO site?
faqs.a: They are on UNESCO's Tentative List, and India has submitted a nomination.

faqs.q: When is the white Rann at its best?
faqs.a: From about November to February, especially on full-moon nights.
